Merchant ventures are sometimes no different from gambling, calculating odds, weighing investment and risk, then staking acceptable capital. Odds are never one hundred percent, so business always involves both gains and losses. 
Kang Zhenzhu dislikes gambling. She believes merchants should wait, observe, and once they obtain reliable information, strike with full force. As long as the information is fresh and true, and operations are proper, the business won't lose money. 
Suli people never make losing deals. 
Back then, she spent the caravan's entire savings to build the Pearl Boat, having secured channels with the Bo Chens, Wutus, and others, all she needed was the protection of the Tang garrison. She heard that army was dirt poor, if a deal could be struck, profits would surely multiply a hundredfold.  
Yet the Tang people actually doubted Suli business acumen? 
"How can you not believe me?" young Kang Zhenzhu blocked Guo Xin at the pass. "Your meager army pay is useless! Invest your army pay silver with me, plus your army's seal, I'll trade jade to the Wutus and return tenfold to you!" 
"Merchant Kang, there are no permanent winning deals in this world." 
"General Guo, you lead troops to victory every day, why not believe I can make a sure profit in business?" 
"Battles can also be lost... If lost, we defend with our lives." 
"..." 
Kang Zhenzhu held back her anger, repeatedly telling herself, "This man was a pass on the Silk Road. She needed to curry favor with the Bo Chen, bribe the Yutu, and never offend the Tang..."  
She put on a smile again: "General, rest assured, not a single coin of tax will be missed! I just want to bring you wealth too..."  
"Even if... even if we really lose money, I'll sell everything I have to compensate you!"  
"Pay the tax, but no investment, no seal loan." Guo Xin's expression didn't change at all.  
Kang Zhenzhu was so worried she felt as if white rabbits were darting around her head, how long could a relationship sustained only by taxes last in this chaotic land?  
That night, Kang Zhenzhu carried a jug of Triphala and climbed onto the city wall. Moonlight stretched the general's shadow long, wine bowls clinked, cup after cup was drunk, "friend" called with each toast, yet finally... Kang Zhenzhu's deal still wasn't struck. Instead, she muddle-headedly signed a new contract with him, she, a wandering Suli merchant, was to fund the digging of wells for the Tang people! Though the wells were for fellow travelers, and the well-watered oasis would be a Suli gathering place, that Han general's talk of the moon and homeland was like unattainable flatbread, who knew if it would be a loss... 
Was Suli money-making skill really going to be buried in the sand this time? Drunk, Kang Zhenzhu leaned against her camel. Hazily, she seemed to see shadows of poplars all over the ground in the moonlight, and suddenly felt... this deal should still be a sure bet.

Years later, floods once again stole the land's vitality. Murky waters spread and receded; the scorching sun baked the mud into hardness. Hunger and death once more stripped people of their dignity. 
Yet, for the first time ever, Mother steamed two white-flour buns and pressed them into Celestial Candle's hands. No matter how her little brother cried and fussed, Mother and Father only gave the buns to her. 
They were the most delicious things Celestial Candle had ever eaten. She couldn't bear to eat them both and tucked one into her clothes. At the same time, a wreath of grass was placed on her head. 
"From now on, learn to behave on your own." "If it hurts, don't cry out. Be obedient." 
Before the bun hidden in her clothes had even cooled, Celestial Candle was led away. She watched as her parents took another girl home. Thinking they had mistaken her for someone else, she cried and struggled desperately. But her parents never looked back. 
It was only many years later that she understood just how much luck was hidden within her misfortune. 
Selling children, trading sons to eat—hunger and death blurred the line between human and beast. 
The old man who bought her sharpened his butcher's knife again and again, then finally sighed. He dropped the knife, picked up a broken bowl and a bamboo staff, and led her west. 
The old man led Celestial Candle across the creek. She was too afraid to take a step. With a stern face, he harshly urged her forward, one careful move at a time. 
Once again, the icy, murky water rose over her feet, then her calves, her waist, her chest... Terrified, she struggled to steady her trembling, fragile body. But as she reached out, her hand found the old man's—quietly hovering just behind her, guarding her all along.
